source: Wang et al. (2025) CogLM: Tracking Cognitive Development of Large Language Models (NAACL)
finding: Benchmark of Piaget-stage abilities. Scores fall as stage rises, in humans and models. GPT-4 reaches about the level of a 20-year-old.
numbers: 1,220 items, 10 abilities, 4 stages. Human check: 207 questionnaires from ages 6-20, 141 valid; age-score Spearman 0.7169, Pearson 0.7362. Overall calibrated accuracy: GPT-4 84.7 (age 20.0), GPT-3.5-Turbo 64.0 (16.1), Llama-2-chat-70B 54.6 (14.1), OPT-6.7B 15.5 (6.5); human 93.7 (21.5).
limits: Multiple choice, authors' own stage mapping. Humans were only ages 6-20 and 'cognitive age' is a fitted mapping. Not a test of Piaget's stage theory itself.
agent_relevance: Background only. LLMs follow a human-like difficulty order, with planning the weak spot.

source: Wang et al. (2025) CogLM: planning and propositional gaps
finding: Even GPT-4 is weak on the plan ability, which humans find easy. GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 beat humans on stage-2 empathy.
numbers: GPT-4 plan 59.4 vs human 95.6. Propositional operation: GPT-4 61.0 vs human 82.0.
limits: Single benchmark, multiple choice.
agent_relevance: A planning step in the scaffold is supported, but the evidence is thin.

source: Wang et al. (2025) CogLM: effect of CoT, self-consistency and tuning
finding: Chain of thought and self-consistency gave almost no gain on GPT-3.5-Turbo's stage scores. Chat tuning (RLHF) raised Llama-2-70B above the text-only model at every stage.
numbers: Self-consistency with 40 samples: overall 64.4 at T=0.3 and 63.1 at T=0.7, against a base near 64.0. Larger parameter count raised scores steadily (OPT 125M to GPT-4).
limits: CoT tested on one model (GPT-3.5-Turbo). Multiple-choice scoring.
agent_relevance: Generic scaffolds may not lift stage-type abilities; scale and tuning did.

source: Wang et al. (2025) CogLM: ablating early abilities and Chain-of-Cognition
finding: Erasing early abilities by prompt hurts later abilities and downstream tasks, as Piaget's order predicts. A Chain-of-Cognition prompt from GPT-3.5 helped a small model a little.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo base GSM8K 59.9 and StrategyQA 65.2; erasing semiotic function dropped GSM8K by 25.5 points. Llama-2-chat-7B averaged 31.0 without and 38.1 with Chain-of-Cognition.
limits: Ablation is done by instruction prompt, so it tests prompt compliance, not removal of a capacity.
agent_relevance: Cheap testable idea: state the needed ability in the prompt. Gain is small.

source: Luo et al. (2025) Vision Language Models Know Law of Conservation without Understanding More-or-Less (ConserveBench)
finding: Vision-language models pass transformational conservation items (reversibility) but fail static more-or-less number items. The two Piagetian supports come apart.
numbers: 365 experiments, 4 quantities, 5 VLMs; all at or below 38% overall. GPT-4o: 97.44% transformational, 31.22% non-transformational single-image, 22.11% number only.
limits: Only 5 models. Workshop paper. No child baseline run in this paper.
agent_relevance: A pass on the classic task can come from shortcuts; test the parts, not only the headline task.

source: Luo et al. (2025) ConserveBench: inverted length-equals-number error
finding: On number items built to elicit the length-equals-number fallacy, GPT-4o when wrong picked the option opposite to the human error.
numbers: 95 non-transformational number tasks; every GPT-4o failure chose the option opposite to the human fallacy.
limits: Authors' interpretation; a counting weakness could explain it.
agent_relevance: Model errors are not child errors, so child stage labels should not be put on model errors.

source: Luo et al. (2026) Vision Language Models Cannot Reason About Physical Transformation (ConservationBench, ICML 2026)
finding: Large test of 112 VLMs. Near chance. Models carry a bias toward 'conserve' and do worse with real images than with blank ones.
numbers: 23,040 questions, 112 VLMs. Accuracy 20-69%, chance 33.3%. Humans 98.35% (6 usable participants). Strict pairwise scoring: 82 of 112 (73.2%) under 10%; only Gemini-2.5-Pro, Doubao-Seed-1.6-Vision and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 beat 33.3%. Conservation vs control accuracy r = -0.510 (n = 112). Conservation accuracy 60% with image vs 85.7% without.
limits: Multiple-choice; human sample is 6 adults.
agent_relevance: Qualifies the optimistic reading of earlier results: passes are driven by a prior toward invariance.

source: Luo et al. (2026) ConservationBench: scale and prompting
finding: Parameter count explains little of conservation accuracy. Frame rate, prompting and curated sampling did not fix it.
numbers: Scale explained R2 = 0.239 in one fit across 112 VLMs (under 24% of variance).
limits: Read from main text only; figures not checked.
agent_relevance: Do not expect scale or generic prompting to fix grounded invariance.

source: Li et al. (2025) Core Knowledge Deficits in Multi-Modal Language Models (CoreCognition)
finding: 12 concepts grouped by Piagetian stage. Models do worse on low-level (sensorimotor, concrete) concepts than high-level ones, and low-level ones scale less.
numbers: 230 models, 11 prompts, 2,530 data points. Reasoning models: no significant gain in 10 of 12 abilities. A cognitive-instruction prompt (p10) raised accuracy by over 6%; most other prompts did not.
limits: Mixed image and video items; the stage grouping is the authors' map.
agent_relevance: Reverse of the child order. Check basics before relying on advanced reasoning.

source: Li et al. (2025) CoreCognition: dependency between stages
finding: In people early abilities underpin later ones. In models, sensorimotor abilities correlate weakly with higher-stage abilities, so the scaffolding is missing.
numbers: Some clusters above 0.65 among high-level abilities; many correlations under 0.4. Core abilities predict public benchmark scores except ChartQA, perspective and intuitive physics.
limits: Correlation across models, not within one model.
agent_relevance: A stage ladder cannot be assumed inside an LLM.

source: Li et al. (2025) CoreCognition: Concept Hacking shortcut test
finding: Swapping the cue that decides the answer shows shortcut use. Almost no model reached equal accuracy on manipulation and control items.
numbers: Control vs manipulation plot (Fig. 11): models fall in a quadrant of high manipulation but below-chance control accuracy, or the reverse; per-model numbers not extracted.
limits: Read from text only.
agent_relevance: A paired control (same item, flipped answer) is the right check for any claimed stage ability.

source: Cowan (2016) Working Memory Maturation: Can We Get at the Essence of Cognitive Growth? (Perspectives on Psychological Science)
finding: Review of whether working memory capacity growth drives development, as neo-Piagetians claim. Strategies, knowledge and attention control also grow, so capacity is not shown to be the driver.
numbers: Gathercole et al. (2004) data: steady rise in span from age 4 to 15. Adults hold about 3-4 chunks; preschool and early school children about 2-2.5 items. Dempster (1978): digit span rose 24% in school years, low-association words only 5%.
limits: Narrative review, not a meta-analysis. Author is sympathetic to capacity theory.
agent_relevance: Chunking and control matter as much as raw capacity when choosing what to scaffold.

source: Cowan (2016) infant versus child discrepancy
finding: Looking-time infant studies show competence far earlier than Piaget claimed, yet reaching tasks fail in 2-year-olds. The gap is linked to task demands.
numbers: Toddlers passed the looking-time surprise test but not the reaching test (Hood et al., 2003; Mash et al., 2006, as cited). Infants hold about 3 items in some studies vs 2-2.5 in preschoolers.
limits: Discrepancy is unresolved in the review.
agent_relevance: The same ability can pass or fail by response format; test the agent in more than one format.

source: Cowan (2016) concluding remarks: capacity versus attention control
finding: Author keeps a role for working-memory growth but says attention control in filling slots is a leading factor in the growth.
numbers: No single effect size; Table 1 lists non-capacity factors (strategies, knowledge, speed, filtering) with studies and findings.
limits: No decisive experiment separates the accounts.
agent_relevance: Attention control is a better scaffold target than raw capacity.

source: Wikipedia: Neo-Piagetian theories of cognitive development (Pascual-Leone, Case, Halford, Fischer, Demetriou)
finding: Lists the rival capacity accounts: Pascual-Leone says mental power grows one unit about every second year; Case adds efficiency; Halford ties stages to relational dimensionality; Demetriou adds domain differences.
numbers: Pascual-Leone: 1 unit at age 2-3 up to 7 at 15. Halford: four structure-mapping levels at about ages 1, 3, 5, 10. Demetriou: spatial capacity 3 units at 6 to 5 at 12; math about 2 to 4; with executive operations about 1 to 3.
limits: Secondary source; figures are from the original authors and were not checked against primary papers.
agent_relevance: The theories give testable limits; Halford's arity limit is the one used in LLM tests.

source: Wikipedia: Conservation (psychology), criticism of research methods
finding: Repeating the same question after the change makes young children switch answers. A naughty-teddy version gave correct conservation at age 4.
numbers: Piaget's threshold 7-11 years; teddy version: four-year-olds showed conservation of matter earlier (no N given on the page).
limits: Secondary summary; no numbers for the teddy study.
agent_relevance: Wording and repeated queries change agent outputs too; ask once and check consistency.

source: Samuel and Bryant (1984) Asking only one question in the conservation experiment (J. Child Psychol. Psychiatry 25:315-318)
finding: Children did better when asked only after the transformation. The fixed-array control gave the most errors.
numbers: Per student summaries in search results: 252 children, about 5 to 8.5 years, three conditions, one-question better at all ages.
limits: Search snippets only; sample and ages not verified from the paper.
agent_relevance: Format effects are large; add a one-question control to any stage test.

source: Rose and Blank (1974), as cited by Samuel and Bryant (1984)
finding: Six-year-olds did much better on conservation of number when asked for a comparison only after the transformation.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Known only from the 1984 abstract in a search result; not opened.
agent_relevance: Same format point as above.

source: Frank et al. (2017) A collaborative approach to infant research (ManyBabies framework, Infancy)
finding: Infant research has small samples and limited measures. The paper proposes large multi-lab replications to estimate how robust key effects are.
numbers: No single result; framework paper.
limits: Abstract and opening read; later sections not read.
agent_relevance: Treat early-competence infant claims with care; effect sizes may shrink.

source: Lucca et al. (2025) Infants' Social Evaluation of Helpers and Hinderers: A Large-Scale, Multi-Lab, Coordinated Replication (Developmental Science)
finding: A large registered replication did not find the infant Helper preference of the original study. A failed replication of an early-competence claim, outside Piaget's physical tasks.
numbers: 37 labs tested 1,018 infants; 567 usable (ages 5.5-10.5 months). Social vs nonsocial condition: BF01 over 100 (informative prior), 10.23 (noninformative); age by condition BF01 8.40 and 7.35. Prior meta-analysis: 0.64 Helper preference, 95% CI [0.60, 0.69]. 44.3% of tested infants excluded.
limits: Video stimuli may give smaller effects than live shows. Domain is social, not Piagetian.
agent_relevance: Warns that 'infants already know X' claims can fail at scale.

source: Halford, Wilson and Phillips (1998) Processing capacity defined by relational complexity (Behav. Brain Sci. 21:803-865)
finding: Capacity is set by the number of related dimensions processed at once; soft limit near one quaternary relation; segmentation and chunking work around it.
numbers: No numbers seen beyond the quaternary limit.
limits: Search snippet level only.
agent_relevance: Source of the arity idea used by the REL benchmark.

source: Anderson, Lebiere, Lovett and Reder (1998) ACT-R: a higher-level account of processing capacity (commentary on Halford et al.)
finding: Rival account. Chunks in the current goal can measure relational complexity, and limits on activation spread set capacity. The quaternary limit fits typical ACT-R goal sizes.
numbers: No new data; says published ACT-R models have goals near four slots.
limits: A commentary; argues compatibility, not a discriminating experiment.
agent_relevance: The arity limit is not unique to Halford; test any scaffold limit instead of assuming it.

source: Andrews, Birney and Halford (2006) Relational processing and working memory capacity in comprehension of relative clause sentences (Memory and Cognition 34:1325-1340)
finding: Three studies of adults. Relational-processing tests predicted comprehension of object-relative sentences before and after controlling for subject-relatives. Working memory tests predicted it only before that control.
numbers: Three experiments; 16 sentence types; relational tasks were premise integration and Latin square; WM tasks were reading span and digit span. Sample sizes not extracted.
limits: Adults only; authors include the theory's proponent.
agent_relevance: Supports relational load over plain span as the limit, matching the arity result for LLMs.

source: Fesser et al. (2026) Evaluating Relational Reasoning in LLMs with REL (ICML 2026)
finding: Frontier LLM accuracy falls steadily as relational complexity rises, with entity count held fixed. More test-time compute or in-context examples did not remove the drop.
numbers: REL-A (Raven matrices, tensors): accuracy down 45% as RC goes 3 to 9. REL-B1: down 93% as RC goes 5 to 20. REL-C (3,016 chemistry questions): completion C1 65.7%, C2 38.1%, C3 26.0%, a 39.7% drop. Token budgets 4,096 to 16,384 changed completion by 0.4% on average; one-shot ICL gave C1 77.0% (+6.6%), C2 43.3% (+3.4%), C3 32.7% (+6.0%).
limits: Three science domains and a few frontier models; RC is the authors' operationalisation, not a test of Halford's age limits.
agent_relevance: Best direct LLM test of a neo-Piagetian construct. Suggests splitting high-arity relations into steps.

source: Xiao et al. (2026) Evaluating Developmental Cognition Capabilities of LLMs (Kegan-based DSCT)
finding: Stage-like labels in sentence completions can be recovered by LLMs. Larger and newer models write text rated at higher developmental stages. Authors do not claim person-level stage.
numbers: 20-item test; fair human-LLM agreement on real responses, stronger within a neighbourhood than exact; exact figures not extracted.
limits: Adult developmental theory (Kegan), not Piaget; abstract read closely only.
agent_relevance: Weak link. Do not use text-based stage labels to claim agent ability.
